# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What Is the KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, inference proceeds autoregressively—generating one token at a time, with each new token depending on all previous tokens. During this process, the model computes key and value vectors for every input token through self-attention. The KV cache stores these computed key-value pairs, preventing redundant recomputation when generating subsequent tokens.

Without caching, generating each new token would require recalculating keys and values for the entire context history, creating quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length. The KV cache reduces this to linear complexity per token by storing pre-computed attention projections.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Long-context scenarios expose critical bottlenecks in naive autoregressive generation. When processing sequences of 32K or 128K tokens, the difference between O(n²) and O(n) per-token computation becomes substantial—not just in FLOPs, but in memory bandwidth and latency. The KV cache transforms an otherwise prohibitive operation into a constant-time attention lookup against stored values.

However, KV caching introduces tradeoffs. Memory usage grows linearly with context length and batch size, since every position's key and value vectors must persist in GPU memory. For very long contexts, this memory pressure can exceed device capacity. Techniques like grouped-query attention, key-value compression, and selective caching strategies have emerged to address these constraints while preserving the fundamental efficiency gains that make long-context inference practical.

The KV cache remains foundational because it directly addresses the computational bottleneck that would otherwise render extended context windows computationally intractable.

# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, inference requires computing attention between tokens. For each new token generated, the model must calculate attention scores against all previous tokens in the sequence. This involves projecting token embeddings into **key** (K) and **value** (V) vectors through learned linear transformations.

KV cache is an optimization that stores these pre-computed K and V vectors for previously processed tokens, avoiding redundant recomputation during autoregressive generation. Instead of recalculating keys and values from scratch for every forward pass, the model retrieves cached vectors and only computes them for newly added tokens.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

As context length increases, the computational cost of attention grows quadratically with sequence length. Without caching, generating each subsequent token would require reprocessing the entire prefix—a prohibitive expense for applications like extended document analysis, multi-turn conversations, or code repositories.

KV cache transforms this quadratic complexity into something closer to linear scaling. Once initial tokens are processed and their representations stored, each new token requires computation proportional only to itself plus a constant-time lookup from the cache. This enables practical deployment of models handling contexts from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Beyond efficiency, KV cache reduces memory bandwidth pressure and enables techniques like prefix caching, where common prompt structures (system instructions, few-shot examples) are computed once and reused across multiple requests—critical for production systems serving many users with overlapping context patterns.
